Hetu: The Intersubjective Consensus Machine Hetu Team
February 10, 2025

Abstract
Blockchain technologies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have transformed digital finance and beyond by enabling decentralized, trust-minimized transactions secured by cryptography and distributed protocols. While blockchains excel in financial applications such as DeFi and NFTs, they face significant limitations, including poor scalability, high costs, and rigid value distribution models that disproportionately reward token holders. These issues become critical in emerging AI-driven scenarios, where complex, resource-intensive pipelines—spanning data collection, training, and inference—demand real-time interactivity and fair contribution attribution. Current blockchain mechanisms like Proof of Work (PoW) and Proof of Stake (PoS) fail to capture the collaborative, off-chain contributions essential for AI development. Hetu introduces Proof of Causality Work (POCW), a novel mechanism that redistributes value based on measurable AI contributions, fostering a sustainable, inclusive, and equitable ecosystem for AI and Web3.

1 Problem Statement: Inequitable Value Distribution of AI
The value distribution problem in AI highlights a fundamental challenge in capturing and rewarding diverse contributions across the AI development lifecycle. Unlike DeFi, where value flows are more straightforward, AI involves a wide variety of contributions—such as data collection, labeling, cleaning, algorithm design, training, fine-tuning, distillation, and inference. These contributions are inherently complex, as it is often difficult to determine whether a single dataset, a training session, or a fine-tuning effort has led to a meaningful improvement, and to quantify the value of that improvement. Most of these contributions occur off-chain, making them invisible to current blockchain-based reward systems. As a result, critical contributions are either undervalued or entirely lost in the rewarding process.

Existing consensus mechanisms, such as Proof of Stake (PoS) [1] and Proof of Work (PoW) [7], exacerbate the issue by concentrating rewards and governance power in the hands of token-holding whales. These mechanisms fail to account for the nuanced and collaborative nature of AI creation, where value is driven by cumulative and interdependent contributions. Whales, who contribute little beyond holding tokens, capture the majority of the value, while smaller contributors—who provide the data, training, and technical expertise that drive real progress—are left unrewarded. Without a decentralized solution that fairly evaluates and rewards contributions based on their actual impact, the promise of equitable value distribution in AI remains unfulfilled.

2 The Intersubjective Consensus
The root cause of the mismatch between the current blockchain model and these emerging scenarios lies in the fundamental principle behind blockchain. All existing blockchains are built upon objective consensus. In objective consensus, the truth is deterministic and universally agreed upon by all participants. The design of these systems ensures that, regardless of who the participants are, given the same predefined conditions and rules, the system will always arrive at the same conclusion. This principle is foundational in many blockchain systems today. For instance, slashing penalties are applied based on incorrect state transitions, or block validity is verified using the hash of the previous block and the transactions it contains.

However, objective consensus has its limitations. One of the biggest ones is that it depends on predefined conditions and rules. The trust we place in blockchain systems hinges on the security and correctness of their underlying tools and frameworks. However, this trust holds only as long as these implementations remain secure. Any cryptographic function bug or mechanism design flaw could lead to severe breaches. With sufficient economic (51% attack) and technical resources, exploiting these vulnerabilities becomes feasible, potentially compromising the system. Moreover, as computational capabilities evolve, even what we consider secure today might not hold under future technological shifts, challenging the very foundations of our consensus mechanisms and cryptographic assurances.

In blockchains, apart from challenges that can be objectively encoded, there are greater issues that are inherently subjective. For instance, fork choice, governance, and protocol upgrades are all subjective decisions that cannot be objectively encoded. These decisions are made by the community, and the collective agreement of the participants determines the outcome. However, the current blockchain systems do not provide a mechanism to handle these subjective decisions. As a result, these decisions are often made off-chain, leading to centralization and fairness issues.

Outside objectivity, there is a complex coordination game that is played out by the participants. This coordination game is inherently subjective, as it involves the beliefs, values, and preferences of the participants. In the current world, long-term value is also created by the subjective beliefs of the participants. To overcome the limitations of objective consensus, a social but rational view of any system can be attributed by intersubjectivity.

We therefore propose a novel form of consensus, termed intersubjective consensus. Instead of objective conditions and rules, decisions in intersubjective consensus are made by the collective agreement of the participants. The process reflects the collective, subjective agreement of all network participants. More critically, intersubjective consensus enables agreement on propositions that are inherently non-objective, such as the value of data, performance of ML models, and quality of inference results, all of which are common in emerging AI scenarios.

3 Hetu Solution: Proof of Causality Work (POCW)
Hetu introduces Proof of Causality Work (POCW) to address the inequities in value distribution and governance within Web3 and AI ecosystems. Unlike traditional mechanisms like Proof of Stake (PoS) and Proof of Work (PoW), which disproportionately reward token-holding whales, POCW ties rewards and governance power to measurable contributions. Causality, in this context, refers to the influence that one contribution has on subsequent actions within the network. For example, if a developer contributes an algorithm that enables further improvements by others, or if a dataset drives meaningful model advancements, these ripple effects are tracked and quantified as causality work. Contributors who generate significant causal influence—by enabling progress through their work—are recognized and rewarded accordingly.

POCW functions by measuring the causal impact of contributions across the ecosystem and redistributing rewards dynamically. Contributions with greater cascading effects—those that drive further actions or innovations—are weighted higher, ensuring that value flows to those who add the most measurable impact. Influential contributors with a history of meaningful work gain higher causality scores, which also tie into governance power, ensuring that decision-making is driven by those who have proven their ability to create value. Passive token holders, by contrast, see diminishing rewards over time, breaking the current cycle of speculation and whale dominance.

Through this mechanism, POCW ensures that off-chain contributions—such as data collection, labeling, training, and fine-tuning—are fairly evaluated and rewarded. By tracking the propagation of contributions across platforms and chains, POCW creates transparency and empowers smaller contributors to participate meaningfully. Governance is similarly redefined, with power anchored to sustained, impactful contributions rather than token holdings, ensuring that only those with a proven track record of creating value influence key decisions. This alignment of rewards and governance with real work fosters trust, incentivizes participation, and eliminates exploitative behaviors by whales seeking short-term gains.

POCW addresses the challenges outlined in the problem statement by capturing the complex, collaborative nature of AI creation, where contributions are cumulative and interdependent. It redistributes value fairly, ensuring that contributors who drive real progress—whether through data, algorithms, or community engagement—are rewarded, while whales who contribute little beyond holding tokens lose influence. This model reflects the interconnected nature of AI development, incentivizing collaboration and fostering a sustainable, inclusive, and community-driven ecosystem. By introducing POCW, Hetu redefines value distribution in AI and Web3, creating a system where rewards are tied to real impact, governance is equitable, and innovation thrives.

We now elaborate our concrete design of POCW in Hetu.

3.1 Causality Graph
Blockchains organize all transactions into a single global sequence. This global order of transactions is arbitrarily determined by miners, proposers, and the consensus protocol. Instead, Hetu orders events in a decentralized network using the natural causal relationship [4]. As discussed previously, causality in the context of Hetu means "potential influence of knowledge". For instance, suppose a node A sends a message to a node B, the message conveys some knowledge of or information about A. All subsequent actions of B, therefore, are potentially influenced by such knowledge. We then define that all following actions of B happened causally after this messaging event, and by extension, all events on A preceding the messaging event, since they may influence the generation of such knowledge.

Such causal ordering forms naturally in any distributed computation which involves message passing. For instance, in an AI pipeline, user data are sent to GPU nodes which generate model weights; base models are fine tuned to produce specialized models; an edge device receives a specialized model to output inference tokens. Causality then defines the following causal order: data → base model → specialized model → inference results. Critically, establishing such causal ordering does not require any external protocols or mechanisms — it is inherent in the computational process. This is key to achieve ordering with minimal cost and latency.

Hetu's causal ordering is formally a partial order relation. This is fundamentally different from a traditional blockchain, in which any two finalized transactions have an ordering. In Hetu, some events are not ordered, i.e., no one can determine which event happens first; such events are exactly those with no causal relationships. The existence of causally unrelated events is commonplace in distributed applications. For example, multiple independent AI agents can generate text outputs without any cross-agent interaction; their actions then have no causal relationships. Note that even though these causally independent events may occur at different physical times, in Hetu, we simply treat these events as concurrent. Partial ordering is therefore critical to the scalability of Hetu: Hetu only needs to establish ordering for events with causal relationships. This causal ordering relation can be represented graphically as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which we term the Hetu causality graph.

3.2 Logical Clocks for Building Causality Graph
To establish and evaluate causal relationships in distributed computation, Hetu designs a logical clock protocol. Each participating node maintains a local logical clock, represented as a vector of integer values [6]. On every local event, the node increments its own clock to reflect local causal influence. When sending messages, the node attaches its latest local clock, and the receiving node merges the attached clock with its local version (using an element-wise max operator) to reflect influence from the sender. The protocol also ensures transitivity in causal ordering across multiple interacting nodes. To deduce the causal relationship between any two events, their attached logical clocks are compared element-wise. Two events are causally independent if not all elements in their clock vector have the same comparison result.

Adversarial participants, however, can manipulate their clock values or deviate arbitrarily from the clock update protocol to violate causal ordering guarantees in Hetu. To tolerate adversarial behaviors, Hetu constructs a verifiable logical clock (VLC). A novel property of VLC is its verifiability. Each VLC is accompanied by a proof that is verifiable by any third party. By validating the proof, any node can be convinced that the attached VLC is correctly generated by a sequence of clock operations. Moreover, the proof verifies that each clock input to the sequence of operations is also correct. This recursive verifiability is very powerful: It gives VLC the same causality properties as previous logical clocks, even in the presence of adversarial participants [5]. Hetu supports multiple concrete implementations of VLC. The most secure version of VLC uses incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) [8], an advanced cryptographic construct. A more efficient version of VLC performs clock updates in TEE hardware and uses TEE attestation as clock proofs.

3.3 Value Distribution Using Hetu Causality Graph
Hetu's causality graph and verifiable logical clock offer an elegant solution to the value distribution problem in Web3. The Hetu causality graph tracks all the causal dependencies within a distributed computation. This set of causal dependencies naturally represents the set of participants contributing to the final computational result. Strong verifiability ensures that no entity, including adversaries, can remove, add, or modify the set of contributors, ensuring fairness. Obviously, tracking the ever growing causality graph is not a scalable, realistic solution. Our verifiable logical clock compresses the causality information into small, bounded-sized structures. Since our logical clock is generated and tagged along during communication, no additional coordination protocol, such as consensus or reliable broadcast [2], is required to produce this verifiable causality graph. These properties allow us to offer fair, secure, and efficient value distribution without any centralized trust.

4 Hetu Technical Stack
As shown in Figure 3, the Hetu technical stack consists of two major components: a TEE-enhanced DAG-based chain [3], and a causality-based value distribution layer.

Hetu Chains: Validators in the Hetu Chain use a Byzantine reliable broadcast [2] protocol to disseminate transaction blocks. A key innovation of our reliable broadcast protocol is leveraging our verifiable logical clock to establish a causal graph among disseminated transaction blocks. The order of transaction blocks naturally follows the causal ordering of the causality graph; all validators reach an agreement on the same transaction order without running a separate consensus protocol. Using TEE, validators establish Byzantine-resistant, verifiable causal relationships with minimum performance overhead. By eliminating a dedicated consensus protocol altogether, the Hetu Chain achieves high transaction throughput and protocol scalability. Moreover, we develop a causality-based speculative execution protocol atop the DAG chain to provide real-time transaction finality.

Value Distribution Layer: A major component of Hetu is a causality-based value distribution layer, as illustrated in Figure 4. The layer exposes a P2P communication stack to applications and infrastructure. Beyond traditional P2P communication primitives, the Hetu stack automatically establishes verifiable logical clocks throughout the communication process. Proofs and verification of the logical clocks are done inside our TEE infrastructure. These clocks are used as input proofs for rewards or slashing in smart contracts on the Hetu Chain. The distribution layer also includes a decentralized graph database. The database stores logical clocks generated in the P2P network and produces complete causality graphs. Developers can submit queries to the graph database to calculate contribution points for each participant in their network. Causality graph analysis can also generate reputation points for any network entity, and these reputation points can be leveraged in the POCW protocol.

5 Application Scenarios

5.1 ModelDAOs for Science
One key application of Hetu is advancing scientific modeling through decentralization. Hetu facilitates the creation of cutting-edge scientific models—such as climate simulations, ecological systems analysis, or disease prediction models—via decentralized, coordinated processes that incorporate fair value distribution. A decentralized approach empowers the creation of robust scientific models by leveraging the collective expertise of a global scientific community, removing centralized bottlenecks that typically restrict access to resources, collaboration, and innovation. Through Hetu, scientists and contributors can participate in data curation, model refinement, and validation processes while being fairly rewarded for their contributions.

Hetu's fair value distribution mechanisms ensure all contributions are transparently recorded and verifiable through its causality graph, which tracks every interaction and dependency across the modeling process. Whether a contribution is focused on data collection, algorithm development, or simulation validation, the contributions are documented and rewarded with non-transferable contribution points. Such transparency not only ensures equitable compensation throughout the modeling lifecycle but also motivates greater collaboration by aligning incentives with a contributor's tangible impact rather than initial capital investment.

At the heart of this framework lies the modelDAO, a decentralized entity that coordinates and governs the scientific modeling process. Within the modelDAO, contributions are tokenized as non-transferable "contribution points," which serve as a proportional measure of influence and reward. Smart contracts handle the automated allocation of rewards, ensuring that the value derived from the development of scientific models is equitably distributed among the contributors. The result is a self-sustaining system that actively drives iterative improvements, fosters interdisciplinary collaboration, and rewards diverse expertise.

By democratizing decision-making, Hetu enables model transparency and reproducibility, two key principles of decentralized science (DeSci). The open and decentralized nature of Hetu ensures that scientific models—along with their underlying data and methodologies—are accessible to the wider community, allowing researchers to validate, refine, and build upon prior work. Hetu also eliminates the proprietary barriers that characterize centralized modeling ecosystems, fostering innovation in critical domains such as public health, climate studies, and energy optimization.

Through Hetu, DeSci gains a powerful tool for achieving its goals of open, inclusive, and equitable scientific advancement. By enabling transparent collaboration, equitable compensation, and robust decentralized governance, modelDAOs provide an innovative solution to many of the challenges faced by traditional, centralized scientific workflows. With Hetu as the foundation, scientific modeling becomes not only more efficient but also more aligned with the values of open science and global accessibility.

5.2 Engagement-Based Governance
In today's decentralized landscape, token-based governance models have shown significant flaws—chief among them, the concentration of power in the hands of wealthy holders, which undermines fairness and broad community participation. One application of Hetu is a new form of governance which shifts the focus from mere token accumulation to genuine, contribution-based engagement. Instead of allowing token purchases to dictate influence, the model awards governance power based on measurable contributions that reflect a participant's true impact on the community, ensuring that decisions are made by those who actively drive growth and innovation.

At the heart of this new governance model is a nuanced understanding of contributions as immutable, heterogeneous, intersubjective, and causally dependent inputs that shape the ecosystem over time. Each contribution, whether it's code development, strategic discussions, or community-building efforts, is recorded as a non-transferable point—a permanent testament to a participant's influence. This design not only provides a more accurate reflection of individual impact but also creates a transparent and audit-friendly framework, decoupling governance authority from economic stake and mitigating risks like bribery and centralization.

Leveraging the power of advanced AI, our system introduces "AI Native" contribution tracking to ensure efficiency, fairness, and scalability. AI agents autonomously evaluate and record diverse forms of participation, acting as trusted "watchdogs" that distribute values to contributions in real time. By integrating cutting-edge security measures such as trusted execution environments and zero-knowledge proofs, the AI-enhanced system guarantees that all contributions are accurately and securely documented, enabling a dynamic, adaptive governance process that grows with the community's needs.

6 Conclusion
Hetu is designed to address the intrinsic inequities of conventional consensus mechanisms. By introducing intersubjective consensus and our novel Proof of Causality Work (POCW), Hetu transcends the limitations of token-centric models and static value distribution. In particular, Hetu tracks the dynamic, causally linked contributions that propel AI and decentralized ecosystems forward—be it through data collection, model training, or algorithmic innovation.

Hetu's robust causality graph, enabled by novel verifiable logical clocks, lays the foundation for a scalable, secure, and equitable infrastructure. This is not a protocol confined to a single application; rather, it has the potential to redefine a wide spectrum of decentralized ventures—from modelDAOs that democratize AI for science to governance systems that reward genuine engagement over speculative accumulation.

By anchoring rewards and influence to measurable impact rather than mere token holdings, Hetu reimagines the economic and operational fabric of both AI and Web3 ecosystems. We believe that this shift will foster an environment where innovation thrives, collaboration is incentivized, and every contribution—no matter how nuanced—finds its rightful recognition. As such, Hetu is poised to become a foundational layer not only for financial applications but for any domain where fair, transparent, and causally driven collaboration is essential in the years to come.
